analysis.one_liner: Requires federal health and environmental agencies to prove a rule's benefits justify its costs before issuing major safety protections.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: it sat in three House committees and their subcommittees from early 1995 until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required nine federal agencies — including the EPA, OSHA, and the Consumer Product Safety Commission — to run formal risk assessments and cost-benefit analyses before issuing any 'major' health, safety, or environmental rule (one affecting the economy by $25 million or more), and to show that a rule's benefits justify its costs [S2][S3]. It also would have created a new Office of Risk Assessment and Cost-Benefit Analysis inside each agency and required agencies to identify the least costly regulatory option and justify choosing anything else [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to three House committees and several subcommittees and never received a hearing outcome, a committee vote, or a floor vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Industries regulated by the EPA, OSHA, and other health and safety agencies. The bill would have given them new procedural hurdles to challenge and delay protective rules, and the requirement that benefits 'justify' costs could have stopped or weakened rules that protect workers, consumers, and communities from pollution and hazards [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated chemical, energy, and manufacturing firms

how_it_helps.text: Before issuing any major rule, each covered agency would have had to demonstrate that the benefits to human health or the environment justify the costs, a test that could block rules whose dollar-quantified benefits fall short of compliance costs [S2][S3].
Agencies would have had to publish, with every final rule, the most flexible and cost-effective regulatory option and justify in writing why they chose anything stronger [S2][S3].

Each agency would have had to create a new Office of Risk Assessment and Cost-Benefit Analysis, apply external peer review, and follow agency-issued risk assessment guidelines before issuing major rules — layers of procedure that add time and opportunity for pushback [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers, consumers, and people living near pollution sources, who would bear the cost of slower, weaker, or abandoned protective rules; and taxpayers, who would fund the new offices, analyses, and reporting the bill requires.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers, consumers, and communities exposed to hazards

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith case for the bill: public and private resources are limited, and its findings argue agencies have not based priorities on actual risk, so ranking threats and targeting the biggest risks first could buy more health protection per dollar [S3].

The bill's own savings provision states it would not modify any existing legal standard designed to protect health, safety, or the environment, so its effect would fall on new discretionary rulemaking rather than overturning current protections [S3].

The cost an honest supporter would acknowledge: converting avoided deaths and illnesses into dollar figures is scientifically and ethically contested, and a benefits-must-justify-costs test skews every borderline call against issuing a protective rule [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill mixes a genuine efficiency argument — rank risks and spend scarce resources where they do the most good — with a mechanism that would have made it harder and slower to issue major health, safety, and environmental protections, shifting the burden onto the agencies and away from regulated firms. Its savings clause limits damage to existing statutory standards, but the new analytical and procedural requirements would apply to future rulemaking across nine agencies. Weighed honestly, the main beneficiaries of passage would have been regulated industries, and the main cost would have fallen on the people those rules protect.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 1995, split among three House committees and then sent to five subcommittees, and none of them ever reported it out, so it died quietly when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dick Zimmer introduced the bill on January 25, 1995, with no cosponsors [S1][S4].
The Speaker referred it to three committees — Government Reform and Oversight, Science, and Commerce — whose jurisdictions covered different parts of the bill [S5].
Within a month it was sent onward to five subcommittees, including subcommittees on regulatory affairs, energy and power, health and environment, and hazardous materials [S5].
No committee or subcommittee ever took further action, and no vote was ever held in either chamber before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who depend on EPA, OSHA, and consumer product protections are better off, because the bill that would have added a cost-justification hurdle to those rules never advanced. Regulated industries also lost nothing they had, but gained nothing they wanted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People protected by existing health and safety rules

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and drew zero cosponsors from either party [S4], so no partisan split appears in the record; the sponsor was a Republican introducing it into a House that Republicans had just taken control of.

industries.industry: Chemical, energy, and heavy manufacturing firms regulated by the EPA
industries.note: The bill would have required benefits to justify costs before any major environmental rule and forced agencies to justify choosing anything beyond the cheapest option, giving regulated firms procedural grounds to delay or dilute rules like air and water pollution limits [S2][S3]. The public cost would be slower or weaker environmental protection.

industries.industry: Employers subject to OSHA workplace safety rules
industries.note: OSHA was a covered agency, so major workplace safety rules would have needed cost-benefit justification and peer review before issuance, raising the bar against rules that protect workers [S2][S3].

The Consumer Product Safety Commission was covered, so major product safety rules would have faced the same cost-justification requirement, potentially leaving hazardous products on the market longer [S2][S3].
